opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think there are a few things coming together at once.

First, code is an unusually good domain for AI because it's so verifiable. When you write code, you can run it, test it, and see whether it works. That gives you a tight feedback loop, both for training the models and for the agents themselves at runtime. An agent can write something, execute it, read the error message, and fix it. That iterative loop is exactly what agentic workflows are good at, and it's much harder to get that kind of clean signal in, say, writing an essay or giving legal advice.

Second, there's an enormous amount of high-quality training data. Decades of open-source code, documentation, Stack Overflow discussions, and commit histories, much of it fairly structured and well-labeled. So the foundation models came in with a strong prior about how software works.

Third, and this is the part I find most exciting, the improvement isn't only from bigger models. A lot of it comes from the agentic workflow around the model: planning, tool use, reflection, breaking a big task into smaller steps, and checking its own work. I've been saying for a while that an agentic workflow wrapped around a decent model can often outperform a stronger model used in a single zero-shot pass. Coding is where that's become most visible.

And finally, there's a huge economic pull. Developers are expensive, software is everywhere, and developers themselves are early adopters who are happy to try new tools and give feedback. So a lot of talent and investment has poured in, and the tools have improved very rapidly as a result.

The net effect is that one engineer can now build things in a weekend that used to take a team weeks. I think that changes not just how we write software, but who gets to build software. More people should learn to code, not fewer, because the leverage you get from knowing how to direct these agents is enormous.

r001.rationale: The response says software is everywhere, developers are expensive, and this creates a huge economic pull that attracts talent and investment.

r002.rationale: It says developers are early adopters who try new tools and give feedback, but does not explain that the people building AI coding agents are themselves users of those agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a few things came together at once. The first is just that the models got good enough at reasoning over long contexts that they can hold a real codebase in their head, so to speak, instead of just completing the next line. That shifted the unit of work from a snippet to a task.

The second, and I think this one is underappreciated, is that coding is a domain with a built-in feedback loop. You write code, you run it, you get an error or a passing test. That's an unusually clean signal. In most domains an agent takes an action and has no idea whether it worked. In software, the compiler and the test suite tell you immediately. So agentic workflows, where the model plans, acts, observes, and revises, work especially well here because the observe step is so informative. That's a big part of why coding agents got good before, say, agents for booking travel or doing legal work.

The third thing is tooling. People figured out how to give the model the right affordances: read a file, run a shell command, search the repo, make a targeted edit. Once you give the model tools shaped like how a developer actually works, rather than asking it to emit a whole file from scratch, the reliability goes way up. A lot of the progress over the last couple of years wasn't the base model alone, it was the scaffolding around it.

And then honestly, there's a lot of training data. The internet has decades of code with commit messages, issues, and the fixes that went with them. That's a very rich supervision signal that most other professions never produced.

So if you put those together, strong reasoning, a verifiable environment, good tool design, and abundant data, coding was almost destined to be the first place agents really worked. My guess is the lesson generalizes: wherever you can build a fast, trustworthy feedback loop, agents will get good quickly. Where you can't, it'll be slower.

r001.rationale: The response credits coding agents’ progress to reasoning, feedback loops, tooling, and training data; it does not attribute development resources to coding’s economic value.

r002.rationale: The response discusses developer-shaped tools, but does not say the agents’ developers are users of those agents or that this gives them good product-building instincts.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a combination of better models and a much better workflow around the models. Coding has this wonderful property that you can often check your work. An agent can write some code, run it, see an error message, and then use that feedback to try again. If you have good tests, that gives it an even stronger signal about whether it’s making progress.

That’s very different from asking a language model to generate an entire program correctly in one shot. When you let it inspect the codebase, make a plan, edit a few files, and run tests, you’re giving it a process for correcting its own mistakes. So the model doesn’t have to be perfect at every step to produce a useful result.

I also think coding is a particularly productive place to build these tools because so much of the working environment is already digital. The agent can interact with files, compilers, and tests directly. The harder part is often specifying what we actually want. Passing the tests is useful, but knowing whether you’ve built the right thing still takes judgment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses coding agents’ effectiveness and coding’s suitability for feedback loops, but does not attribute development resources to coding’s large economic value.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that agent developers are users of the agents or connect that experience to product-building instincts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a few things came together. One is that the underlying models got much better at writing code. But the other is that we moved from asking a model to produce the right answer in one shot to giving it a workflow: write some code, run it, look at the error, and fix it.

Coding is particularly well suited to that because you can get feedback from the environment. You have a compiler, you have tests, you can inspect what the program actually does. So the agent has a way to check its work and iterate.

And then there’s the tooling around the model. Giving it access to the right files, letting it search a codebase, letting it execute commands—those capabilities make a big difference. The model is important, but a lot of the progress comes from building a system around it that lets it make progress through multiple steps.

r001.rationale: The candidate credits better models, iterative feedback, and supporting tools, but does not attribute investment in coding agents to coding’s economic value.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses tooling around agents, but does not say their developers are agent users or that this makes them better product builders.
